title: Imaging superconducting weak spots through vortex-assisted THz near-field photovoltage
authors: Sergio J. Salvía-Fernández, Ekaterina Khestanova, Zoe Velluire-Pellat, Leonardo R. Cadorim, Sergi Batlle-Porro, David A. Czaplewski, Johann Osmond, Sebastian Castilla, Adrian Bachtold, Milorad V. Milošević, Aharon Kapitulnik, Frank H. L. Koppens
abstract: Nanoscale inhomogeneities are a defining feature of many superconducting materials, yet their local electromagnetic response has remained difficult to access experimentally. This is because their relevant energy scale lies in the terahertz range, where wavelengths -- on the order of hundreds of microns -- are too large to spatially resolve nanoscopic variations. Here, we demonstrate the first application of THz near-field photovoltage nanoscopy in a superconductor, achieving 300 nm spatial resolution at 2.52 THz. Scanning a current-biased NbN strip, we reveal photovoltage peaks within the bulk associated with nanoscopic defects of reduced superfluid density. The observed photovoltage follows the evolution of the vortex-dissipative state and is attributed to enhanced vortex-antivortex pair nucleation at defect sites. Together, these results open a direct route to probing how material inhomogeneities influence light-matter interactions in superconductors, with implications for superconducting devices and strongly inhomogeneous systems such as high-Tc and moiré materials.
summary: The research pioneers the use of THz near-field photovoltage microscopy to image nanoscale defects within superconductors. By exciting the material with THz radiation, they measure localized voltage peaks that correlate directly with enhanced vortex dynamics at these weak spots. This technique provides a powerful new tool for understanding how material disorder influences superconducting properties.
main_problem: The primary challenge is experimentally probing nanoscale inhomogeneities (weak spots) within superconductors, as their relevant energy scales are in the THz range, which far-field techniques cannot resolve.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that THz near-field photovoltage nanoscopy can map these defects by observing localized photovoltage peaks associated with enhanced vortex-antivortex pair nucleation at defect sites.
method: They employed THz near-field photovoltage nanoscopy using an AFM tip to confine THz radiation, achieving $\sim 300 	ext{ nm}$ spatial resolution while simultaneously measuring the local voltage response under a DC bias current.
model_or_system: The study uses superconducting thin films (e.g., NbN) as the physical system. The physics involves quasiparticle excitation via THz photons, leading to vortex-assisted dissipation and measurable photovoltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{PV}}$). Theoretical support comes from Time-Dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations.
key_observables: Photovoltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{PV}}$) spatial profiles showing localized peaks; the non-monotonic dependence of peak amplitude on bias current ($I_b$); and the constant Full Width at Half Maximum ($	ext{FWHM}$) of these peaks.
important_parameters: THz frequency (2.52 THz, $\hbar\omega = 10.4 	ext{ meV}$), spatial resolution ($\sim 300 	ext{ nm}$), and the superconducting gap energy ($2\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The observed $	ext{V}_{	ext{PV}}$ peak is directly attributed to enhanced vortex-antivortex pair nucleation at sites of reduced superfluid density (defects).
figures_summary: Figures show spatial maps and profiles of the measured $	ext{V}_{	ext{PV}}$, detailing how these peaks appear in the bulk, their dependence on bias current, and confirmation using autocorrelation functions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the technical feasibility by describing the THz near-field setup. It then presents evidence via spatial mapping to locate defects (peaks), followed by analyzing the physics of the signal—showing its correlation with vortex dynamics and comparing results against theoretical TDGL simulations.
why_interesting: This work bridges superconducting theory (vortex dynamics, gap energy) with advanced quantum optics/nano-spectroscopy techniques. The ability to probe local electronic states using THz photons is highly relevant for understanding non-equilibrium quantum phenomena in condensed matter.
